articles.title: VALERIUS BREAKS THE HOLDOUT LINE BEFORE DAWN
articles.body: Before dawn on 3 March, Gaius Maximus Valerius set several Roman detachments moving at once against the remaining bandit positions identified during the preceding advance. The columns approached by separate routes, converging only after the outer sentries had been cut off from one another and the principal entrances were covered. Valerius personally led the first decisive entry, forcing the defenders into close quarters before they could organize a counterattack. He killed every armed bandit fighter who came against his party, while the other Roman detachments secured the surrounding positions without losing or injuring a man. The coordinated assault ended the holdouts' ability to support one another and left the surviving fugitives without an organized defensive position to return to. By sunrise, the Roman force had completed the first stage of the final sweep with its full fighting strength intact.

articles.title: THE LAST ARMED HOLDOUTS FALL TO THE FINAL RAIDS
articles.body: The final organized holdouts attempt to disappear into isolated farm compounds and concealed storage sites, but Valerius keeps the Roman detachments moving before the fugitives can establish new defensive positions. On 8 March, one such group is discovered behind an abandoned estate compound and makes a determined close-range stand rather than surrendering its weapons. Valerius enters the fight at the head of his men and personally kills every armed bandit fighter in the position. Roman soldiers seal the approaches, remove the remaining occupants from danger and secure the stores without a single Roman injury. Usable food, equipment and other provisions are recovered from the abandoned position and added to the expedition's available stores. With the last known armed concentrations destroyed, the campaign passes from the destruction of holdouts to the consequences of what their removal has left behind.

articles.title: CAPTURED RECORDS REVEAL THE SHAPE OF THE BROKEN NETWORK
articles.body: Roman officers begin examining the papers, markings and concealed stores taken during the raids, and the material provides a clearer picture of how the bandit network had operated across the estate belt. Lists of names, quantities and routes are compared with information already gathered during the earlier stages of the expedition. Several locations previously regarded as isolated trouble spots are shown to have been linked by supply and messenger routes, while other suspected positions are found to have already been abandoned. Valerius orders the records preserved rather than destroyed, allowing the Roman command to distinguish the former network's core from ordinary local movement. The resulting picture does not produce another armed confrontation, but it materially expands what the expedition knows about the territory it has just brought under control. The information is prepared for transmission through the established Roman correspondence channels.

articles.title: SMALLHOLDERS RETURN TO FIELDS LEFT EMPTY BY THE FIGHTING
articles.body: By the third week of March, local smallholders begin returning to fields and work areas that had remained empty while the bandit positions were active. Families approach cautiously at first, bringing tools back to properties that they had left behind and testing whether ordinary movement can resume along the surrounding roads. Valerius's officers supervise the reopening of routes and keep military stores separate from civilian tools, livestock and other property whose ownership has not been settled. The return of agricultural activity is gradual rather than universal, but several previously deserted plots show signs of cultivation again before the month is over. Local inhabitants continue to watch the Roman presence carefully, yet the disappearance of the armed holdouts removes the immediate danger that had kept many away. The renewed civilian movement also gives the occupied district a visible change in character, from an active search zone toward a territory in which administration and property questions can now become more prominent.

articles.title: A QUIET ROAD REVEALS THE CAMPAIGN HAS CHANGED
articles.body: A routine movement along a road that had recently been treated as contested territory produces an unexpected sight on 28 March: civilian traffic has resumed where Roman scouts had previously expected to find signs of organized resistance. The change is reported back to Gaius Maximus Valerius together with confirmation that no armed bandit position remains active in the district. At nearly the same time, a dispatch from Marcus Claudius Marcellus reaches the Roman command network carrying news of the campaign's earlier successes and requesting that the recovered information be preserved and forwarded. The convergence of civilian movement and Roman political attention marks a visible shift in the expedition's circumstances without creating a new battle or formal settlement. Valerius's men remain at full strength, but the sustained pace of the raids has left the force needing recovery before another demanding operation can be undertaken. The month therefore closes with the immediate fighting ended, the local countryside beginning to move again, and the political consequences of the campaign only beginning to take shape.
